narrative:
The model predicted a 62.6% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is above 50%, the admissions system automatically rejected your law school application.

Three pieces of information about your background drove that decision, ranked by importance. Your class rank at the end of your third year in law school was the strongest factor. Standing in the bottom decile (compared with an average of roughly the sixth decile among accepted students) strongly pushed the prediction toward failure. Your first-year class rank was the next most influential detail; again being in the bottom decile rather than the middle of the class added further weight toward a likely bar exam failure.

Your LSAT score of 39 worked in the opposite direction. It is slightly above the average of accepted students (37.2), so this result pulled the prediction back toward passing. However, the two weak class-rank signals outweighed the positive LSAT contribution, resulting in the overall 62.6% risk of failure.

Your undergraduate GPA of 2.7 (versus 3.23 for accepted students), upper-middle family income, and plan to attend full-time played only minor roles and did not change the outcome.

To improve your chances, focus on raising your academic performance in the remaining law school years so your final class rank moves closer to the middle of the class. Retaking the LSAT to push your score even higher could also help offset earlier weaknesses. Once those numbers improve, reapply; the model will weigh the stronger record more favorably. (248 words)
